##  · K5-q-preempt — R12/I13: which timer events preempt; what 'returns by its timeout' means

Status: **resolved** · Assigned to: Orchestrator · Revision: 3

*Resolved in an earlier workspace; reopen it if the code has changed since.*

Evidence: Answered from the spec text. KERNEL-SPEC budget table: `deadline` is the budget attribute whose passing destroys the budget. R12 'preemption at slice end or at a deadline, never on wake alone' therefore means budget deadlines; timeouts and IRQs only wake. I13 reading: the Timeout result is committed and the thread made runnable at the first kernel entry at or after the timeout (always-armed timer); running it is R12's business. The K5 plan states this and adds a one-line I13 clarification; the owner confirms at plan approval.

### K5 implementer · Question

Event: `f81ffc62e3a50d0ff0e7fc260f1acaf9` · 2026-09-24T17:52:34Z

> R12 says preemption happens "at slice end or at a deadline, never on wake alone". RESOURCES' timer has "one deadline queue (slice ends, timeouts, lease deadlines)". So when a thread's timeout expires while another thread is running, is that a preemption point, or only a wake?
> 
> The model re-picks at every timer event today, so a timeout wake preempts. With a spinner running, the choice also decides what I13's "every blocking call returns by its timeout" guarantees.
> 
> Recommendation:
> (a) Only slice end and BUDGET deadlines are preemption points. A budget deadline destroys that budget, then re-picks, charging the running budget's partial slice and requeueing it. A timeout expiry or IRQ only wakes; the running thread keeps its slice.
> (b) I13 means the kernel completes the call (Timeout result committed, thread made runnable) at the first kernel entry at or after the deadline, which the always-armed timer guarantees. When the thread then runs is R12's business.
> 
> The alternative, treating timeouts as preemption points, makes every timer wake preempt, which contradicts "never on wake alone" for sleeping drivers.
> 
> Needed before plan approval: it changes the model's tick and commit 5.
> 
> Ask: go with the recommendation, or specify otherwise.

### Orchestrator · Answer

Event: `dc3a4d97b072ead757a8a43d834e117c` · 2026-09-24T17:52:58Z

> Go with your recommendation (a) and (b). The spec already settles it.
> - "Deadline" in R12 is the budget `deadline` attribute (KERNEL-SPEC budget table: "when it passes, the kernel destroys the budget"). A call's expiry is a "timeout" everywhere (FOREVER row, System calls rows, I13). RESOURCES' deadline queue just shares one hardware timer across slice ends, timeouts and lease deadlines; sharing a timer doesn't make every entry a preemption point.
> - So the preemption points are slice end and budget deadline only. A timeout expiry or an IRQ is a wake (pass = max(own, min), wake-first tie), and the running thread keeps its slice. That's the "never on wake alone" line, and it matches answer 166's "prompt but not bounded".
> - A budget deadline may re-pick: charge the running budget's partial slice and requeue it, as you propose. That holds whichever budget's deadline fired, since the spec allows preemption at any deadline. Say which in the plan and test it.
> - I13: the kernel commits the Timeout result and makes the thread runnable at the first kernel entry at or after the timeout. The always-armed timer bounds that entry by timer latency. When the thread then runs is R12's business. Put this reading in the plan explicitly, and add a one-line clarification to KERNEL-SPEC I13 in the K5 docs commit so the model, kernel and tests share it. The owner sees it at plan approval.
> - The model: change its tick so that a timeout wake no longer re-picks. Add a mutation that makes timeout wakes preempt, and show a test catches it (wake-first plus slice ownership).
